question: How do you get the most out of your first year as a Chief member in 2028?
body:
## Direct Answer The members who get the most out of their first year at Chief treat it as a deliberate leadership practice, not a passive perk: they show up to every Core group session, prepare a real challenge for each one, use the community and events between meetings, and set two or three concrete goals they can measure by month twelve. Front-load your effort in the first ninety days, because the relationships and habits you build early compound across the entire membership year. Chief is a private network built for senior women executives — VPs, SVPs, and C-suite leaders — and its center of gravity is the Core group: a small, professionally facilitated peer circle that meets monthly. The platform, digital community, and events wrap around that core. The difference between a member who renews enthusiastically and one who quietly lapses usually is not the quality of the network — it's how intentionally they engaged in year one. This essay lays out how to run that first year like a well-managed operating plan. ## What actually delivers value in a Chief membership — and where does the ROI hide? The visible product is easy to list: a monthly Core group, a guide or executive coach who facilitates it, access to the member community, member-only events and salons, curated content, and clubhouse-style spaces in some cities. But the ROI does not live evenly across those features. The overwhelming majority of durable value comes from two places: the depth of trust you build inside your Core group, and the specific, high-stakes problems you bring to be worked on. Everything else — events, content, the app feed — is amplification. If the Core relationships are shallow, no amount of event attendance compensates. This matters because new members often invert the priority. They RSVP to marquee speaker events, screenshot the highlights, and treat the monthly Core session as the thing they cancel when their calendar gets tight. That is exactly backwards. A single Core session where you put a genuine board-level or people problem on the table — and eight peers who have sat in your chair pressure-test it — is worth more than a dozen fireside chats. The hidden ROI is in vulnerability at altitude: candor between people who have no reporting relationship, no equity conflict, and no reason to flatter you. That's structurally hard to find anywhere else, and it's the reason the membership exists. The second place ROI hides is in the weak-tie network the platform unlocks. Your Core group is eight or so strong ties. The broader member base is thousands of senior women whose introductions, warm paths, and candid vendor or hiring references are a phone call away — but only if you actually reach into the community rather than waiting for it to reach you. Members who post real asks and answer others' asks get pulled into a reciprocity loop; lurkers stay invisible and conclude, wrongly, that "the network didn't do anything for me." ## How should you approach your first 90 days to build momentum? Treat the first quarter as onboarding you run, not onboarding that happens to you. The failure mode is drift: you attend the first Core session, enjoy it, and then let three weeks of operating chaos swallow the intent until the next one. Momentum in a peer network is fragile early and self-sustaining late, so the entire game is getting to self-sustaining fast. Start by writing down, before your first session, the two or three questions you cannot answer alone right now. Not "networking" — specific decisions. *Do I take the COO role or hold out for CEO? How do I manage out a loyal but plateaued VP? Should I raise now or extend runway?* These become the raw material you bring to Core, and having them written keeps you from defaulting to small talk when a facilitator asks what's on your mind. Then make the mechanical commitments that protect the practice: block the Core dates as immovable, introduce yourself in the community with a real bio and a real ask within the first week, and attend at least one event in the first month purely to calibrate what "good" looks like. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Join Chief] --> B[Week 1: Post real bio + one concrete ask] B --> C[Before Session 1: Write 2-3 unsolved decisions] C --> D[Session 1: Bring one real problem, not small talk] D --> E{Momentum check
Day 30} E -->|Engaged| F[Deepen: DM two peers, RSVP one event] E -->|Drifting| G[Recommit: re-block dates, re-post an ask] F --> H[Day 90: Trusted Core + active in community] G --> C H --> I[Compounding value for months 4-12] ``` The ninety-day mark is your first honest checkpoint. By then you should be able to name at least two Core peers you'd text before a big decision, have made or received at least one useful introduction, and have brought at least one real problem to the group. If you can't, you're drifting — and the fix is not "try harder generally," it's to re-run the concrete steps above. For a deeper framework on turning a peer network into measurable outcomes, see the [RevOps guide on operating cadences](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/operating-cadence-rhythm) — the same rhythm discipline that makes a revenue team predictable makes a membership productive. ## How do you get the most out of your Core group specifically? The Core group is the flywheel, so it deserves its own operating discipline. Facilitated peer groups reward preparation and punish passivity in obvious ways: the members who arrive with a sharpened, real problem get an hour of senior counsel; the members who arrive empty get to watch other people get counsel. Over a year, that gap is enormous. Prepare for each session as if it were a board meeting where you are the only agenda item that matters. Bring one problem, framed tightly: the decision, the constraint, what you've already tried, and the specific thing you're stuck on. Resist the urge to bring a problem you've secretly already solved just to look competent — you waste the group and cheat yourself. The most valuable sessions feel slightly uncomfortable because you're exposing something genuinely unresolved. Trust that the room is built for exactly that; the confidentiality norms and the absence of professional conflict are what make it safe. Equally important: be a great group member for others, not just a good extractor of value. Peer groups run on reciprocity, and the members who listen hard, ask sharp questions, and follow up between sessions become the people others invest in. When a peer works through their succession problem in March, check in with them in April. That single act — remembering, following up, closing the loop — is what converts a monthly acquaintance into a genuine ally. Reliability compounds; the person who shows up consistently and remembers becomes the person the whole group protects and promotes. Finally, use the guide or coach who facilitates the group as a resource, not just a timekeeper. They see patterns across many groups and many leaders, and a direct question to them — "where do you see members like me get stuck at this stage?" — often surfaces the most useful insight of the month. ## How do you extend the value beyond the monthly meeting? If your Chief membership only lives inside one hour a month, you're leaving most of it on the table. The membership is designed as an always-on network with periodic high-intensity moments, and the members who win treat the between-meeting space as the real surface area. The monthly session builds the trust; the digital community and one-to-one relationships spend it. The highest-leverage between-meeting move is the direct message. When a peer says something in Core that resonates — or that you disagree with — follow up privately. "That thing you said about managing your board chair stuck with me; can I ask how you handled the follow-up?" These one-to-one threads are where the real relationships form, because Core sessions are necessarily shared and shallow-per-person; DMs go deep on one relationship at a time. Aim to convert at least a few Core acquaintances into people you talk to independently of the scheduled meeting. ```mermaid graph LR A[Monthly Core Session] -->|builds trust| B[1:1 DMs with peers] A -->|surfaces topics| C[Community posts + asks] B --> D[Warm intros] C --> D D --> E[Career moves, hires,
board seats, deals] C -->|patterns| F[Events + salons] F --> B E -->|new problems| A ``` The community platform is the second surface. Treat it like a senior-executive Q&A engine: post the questions that are too sensitive for LinkedIn and too specialized for a general search, and answer others' questions generously so you build a reputation as a giver. Events and salons are the third — but attend them with intent, not FOMO. Pick events by the people likely to be in the room or the specific skill you're trying to build, not by the fame of the headliner. Two people you actually talk to at a small salon beats a thousand-person keynote you watched silently. The through-line connecting all three surfaces is the same discipline that governs any high-performing system: a deliberate cadence and clear ownership, the same principle behind a well-run [revenue rhythm](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revenue-rhythm-cadence). ## How do you measure whether year one actually paid off? "Did I get value?" is too vague to answer honestly, which is why members either over-credit the membership out of sunk-cost loyalty or under-credit it out of vague disappointment. Set measurable intentions at the start and grade against them, the same way you'd hold any investment accountable. The goals don't need to be grand; they need to be specific and checkable. Good first-year goals cluster into a few categories. Relationship goals: *build three peer relationships I'd call before a major career decision.* Decision goals: *get senior counsel on the two hardest calls I face this year.* Career goals: *test whether I'm ready for a board seat / a CEO role / a pivot, using the group as a sounding board.* Skill goals: *close a specific gap — investor relations, executive communication, managing a founder-CEO.* Network goals: *make and receive at least a handful of useful warm introductions.* Write two or three of these down at the start, revisit them at ninety days and again at month nine, and adjust the ones that turned out to be wrong. At renewal time, the honest scorecard is simple: did the membership change any decision, unlock any relationship, or build any capability you would not have gotten otherwise? One genuinely better career decision, informed by peers who'd made the same call, can dwarf the annual cost. If you hit zero on all three categories, the problem is almost always engagement depth in the first quarter, not the network itself — and the fix for year two is the ninety-day discipline above, run harder. For structuring goals you can actually measure, the [outcome-metrics primer](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/outcome-metrics-framework) translates fuzzy intentions into checkable targets. ## What are the most common first-year mistakes, and how do you avoid them? The mistakes are predictable, which is good news — predictable failures are preventable. The first is treating Chief as a conference badge rather than a practice: joining for the signal of belonging, then not doing the work. The signal fades; the practice compounds. Avoid it by committing to the cadence before you commit to the identity. The second mistake is performing competence instead of exposing problems. Senior leaders are conditioned to project having it handled, and that instinct is exactly wrong inside a confidential peer group — it converts the most valuable room you have into another audience to impress. The third is passivity in the community: waiting to be invited, waiting for value to arrive, then concluding the network is quiet. The community is a mirror; it reflects the energy you put in. The fourth is over-indexing on events and under-indexing on the Core group and one-to-one relationships — optimizing for the visible and neglecting the valuable. The fifth is skipping sessions when work gets busy, which is precisely when you most need the counsel and precisely when a missed session does the most damage to your standing in the group. Avoiding all five reduces to one habit: protect the small, high-trust interactions above the large, low-trust ones, and put real problems on the table early. Do that, and year one becomes the foundation the rest of your membership is built on rather than a trial you're ambivalent about renewing. ## Related questions ### Is a Chief membership worth it for a first-year member? It's worth it if you engage deliberately — attend every Core session with a real problem, build a few peer relationships, and set measurable goals. Passive members rarely see the value; active ones often find one better decision pays for the year. ### How much does a Chief membership cost? Chief has historically charged an annual membership fee that varies by tier and city, and companies frequently sponsor executives' memberships. Confirm current pricing directly with Chief, as tiers and fees change over time. ### Who qualifies to join Chief? Chief is designed for senior women executives — typically VP-level and above, including SVPs, C-suite leaders, and founders. Eligibility centers on executive seniority and scope of leadership rather than industry. ### What is a Chief Core group? A Core group is a small, professionally facilitated peer circle of senior women leaders that meets monthly. It's the heart of the membership — a confidential space to work through real leadership challenges with peers who have no conflict of interest. ### How is Chief different from LinkedIn or other networks? Chief is a closed, vetted network of senior women executives built around facilitated peer groups and confidentiality, not open broadcasting. The value is depth and candor among peers at similar altitude, versus reach and self-promotion. ## FAQ **How often does a Chief Core group meet?** Core groups typically meet monthly, guided by a professional facilitator or executive coach. The monthly cadence is the backbone of the membership, so protecting those dates on your calendar is the single most important commitment you make. **What should I bring to my first Core session?** Bring one real, unresolved leadership challenge — a decision you're genuinely stuck on — framed tightly: the situation, what you've tried, and where you're stuck. Preparation is what separates a valuable session from small talk. **Can my company pay for my Chief membership?** Yes. Many members have their memberships sponsored by their employer as an executive development and retention investment. It's worth asking your company whether leadership development budget can cover it. **How much time does Chief realistically require?** Plan for the monthly Core session plus a few hours a month in the community, one-to-one conversations, and occasional events. The floor is the Core meeting; members who add even a few hours of between-meeting engagement get disproportionately more value. **What if I don't click with my assigned Core group?** Give it a few sessions, since trust in peer groups builds over time and early awkwardness is normal. If the fit still feels wrong after genuine effort, talk to your guide or Chief's member support about options — don't just quietly disengage. **Is Chief only useful for women in specific industries?** No. Chief spans industries and functions; the common thread is executive seniority, not sector. That cross-industry mix is a feature — peers from outside your industry often give the clearest read on your problem precisely because they aren't inside it. **How do I keep momentum after the first few months?** Set measurable goals at the start, check them at ninety days and again mid-year, and convert Core acquaintances into one-to-one relationships through direct follow-up. Momentum comes from the between-meeting work, not just the sessions. **What's the biggest mistake first-year members make?** Treating the membership as a passive perk instead of an active practice — attending events while skipping the deep Core work, and performing competence rather than exposing real problems. Engagement depth in the first quarter determines the entire year. ## Sources - [Chief — Official Site](https://chief.com/) - [Chief — How It Works](https://chief.com/how-it-works) - [Harvard Business Review — Peer Coaching and Executive Development](https://hbr.org/) - [McKinsey — Women in the Workplace Report](https://www.mckinsey.com/featured-insights/diversity-and-inclusion/women-in-the-workplace) - [Center for Creative Leadership — The Value of Peer Networks](https://www.ccl.org/) - [Forbes — Executive Peer Networks and Leadership](https://www.forbes.com/) - [LeanIn.Org — Women in Leadership Research](https://leanin.org/) - [Harvard Business Review — What Makes a Good Mentor and Sponsor](https://hbr.org/) ## Related on PULSE - [Operating cadence and leadership rhythm](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/operating-cadence-rhythm) - [Revenue rhythm and meeting cadence](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revenue-rhythm-cadence) - [Outcome-metrics framework for measurable goals](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/outcome-metrics-framework) - [Building high-trust executive relationships](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/executive-relationship-building)
